L29:     * cite1†latest L30: # Memory Allocation
L31: 
L32: Vulkan memory is broken up into two categories, host memory and device memory.
L33: ## Host Memory
L34: 
L35: Host memory is memory needed by the Vulkan implementation for non-device-visible storage.
L36: 
L37:  | This memory may be used to store the implementation’s representation and state of Vulkan objects.
L38: Vulkan provides applications the opportunity to perform host memory allocations on behalf of the Vulkan implementation. If this feature is not used, the implementation will perform its own memory allocations. Since most memory allocations are off the critical path, this is not meant as a performance feature. Rather, this can be useful for certain embedded systems, for debugging purposes (e.g. putting a guard page after all host allocations), or for memory allocation logging.
L39: Allocators are provided by the application as a pointer to a `VkAllocationCallbacks` structure:
L40: 
L41:     `// Provided by VK_VERSION_1_0
L42:     typedef struct VkAllocationCallbacks {
L43:         void*                                   pUserData;
L44:         PFN_vkAllocationFunction                pfnAllocation;
L45:         PFN_vkReallocationFunction              pfnReallocation;
L46:         PFN_vkFreeFunction                      pfnFree;
L47:         PFN_vkInternalAllocationNotification    pfnInternalAllocation;
L48:         PFN_vkInternalFreeNotification          pfnInternalFree;
L49:     } VkAllocationCallbacks;`
L50:   * `pUserData` is `NULL` or an application-defined user data pointer to be interpreted by the implementation of the callbacks. When any of the callbacks in `VkAllocationCallbacks` are called, the Vulkan implementation will pass this value as the first parameter to the callback. This value can vary each time an allocator is passed into a command, even when the same object takes an allocator in multiple commands.
L51:   * `pfnAllocation` is a cite9†PFN_vkAllocationFunction pointer to an application-defined memory allocation function.
L52: 
L53:   * `pfnReallocation` is a cite10†PFN_vkReallocationFunction pointer to an application-defined memory reallocation function.
L54: 
L55:   * `pfnFree` is a cite11†PFN_vkFreeFunction pointer to an application-defined memory free function.
L56:   * `pfnInternalAllocation` is a cite12†PFN_vkInternalAllocationNotification pointer to an application-defined function that is called by the implementation when the implementation makes internal allocations.
L57: 
L58:   * `pfnInternalFree` is a cite13†PFN_vkInternalFreeNotification pointer to an application-defined function that is called by the implementation when the implementation frees internal allocations.
L59: 
L60: Valid Usage
L61:   * VUID-VkAllocationCallbacks-pfnAllocation-00632
L62: `pfnAllocation` must be a valid pointer to a valid application-defined cite9†PFN_vkAllocationFunction L63: 
L64:   * VUID-VkAllocationCallbacks-pfnReallocation-00633
L65: `pfnReallocation` must be a valid pointer to a valid application-defined cite10†PFN_vkReallocationFunction L66: 
L67:   * REDACTED
L68: `pfnFree` must be a valid pointer to a valid application-defined cite11†PFN_vkFreeFunction L69:   * VUID-VkAllocationCallbacks-pfnInternalAllocation-00635
L70: If either of `pfnInternalAllocation` or `pfnInternalFree` is not `NULL`, both must be valid callbacks
L71: The type of `pfnAllocation` is:
L72: 
L73:     `// Provided by VK_VERSION_1_0
L74:     typedef void* (*PFN_vkAllocationFunction)(
L75:         void*                                       pUserData,
L76:         size_t                                      size,
L77:         size_t                                      alignment,
L78:         VkSystemAllocationScope                     allocationScope);`
L79: 
L80:   * `pUserData` is the value specified for cite14†VkAllocationCallbacks ::`pUserData` in the allocator specified by the application.
L81:   * `size` is the size in bytes of the requested allocation.
L82: 
L83:   * `alignment` is the requested alignment of the allocation in bytes and must be a power of two.
L84: 
L85:   * `allocationScope` is a cite15†VkSystemAllocationScope value specifying the allocation scope of the lifetime of the allocation, as described cite16†here .
L86: If `pfnAllocation` is unable to allocate the requested memory, it must return `NULL`. If the allocation was successful, it must return a valid pointer to memory allocation containing at least `size` bytes, and with the pointer value being a multiple of `alignment`.
L87:  | Correct Vulkan operation cannot be assumed if the application does not follow these rules. For example, `pfnAllocation` (or `pfnReallocation`) could cause termination of running Vulkan instance(s) on a failed allocation for debugging purposes, either directly or indirectly.
L88: In these circumstances, it cannot be assumed that any part of any affected cite17†VkInstance objects are going to operate correctly (even cite18†vkDestroyInstance ), and the application must ensure it cleans up properly via other means (e.g. process termination).
L89: If `pfnAllocation` returns `NULL`, and if the implementation is unable to continue correct processing of the current command without the requested allocation, it must treat this as a runtime error, and generate cite19†VK_ERROR_OUT_OF_HOST_MEMORY at the appropriate time for the command in which the condition was detected, as described in cite20†Return Codes .
L90: If the implementation is able to continue correct processing of the current command without the requested allocation, then it may do so, and must not generate cite19†VK_ERROR_OUT_OF_HOST_MEMORY as a result of this failed allocation.
L91: The type of `pfnReallocation` is:
L92: 
L93:     `// Provided by VK_VERSION_1_0
L94:     typedef void* (*PFN_vkReallocationFunction)(
L95:         void*                                       pUserData,
L96:         void*                                       pOriginal,
L97:         size_t                                      size,
L98:         size_t                                      alignment,
L99:         VkSystemAllocationScope                     allocationScope);`
L100:   * `pUserData` is the value specified for cite14†VkAllocationCallbacks ::`pUserData` in the allocator specified by the application.
L101: 
L102:   * `pOriginal` must be either `NULL` or a pointer previously returned by `pfnReallocation` or `pfnAllocation` of a compatible allocator.
L103: 
L104:   * `size` is the size in bytes of the requested allocation.
L105: 
L106:   * `alignment` is the requested alignment of the allocation in bytes and must be a power of two.
L107:   * `allocationScope` is a cite15†VkSystemAllocationScope value specifying the allocation scope of the lifetime of the allocation, as described cite16†here .
L108: If the reallocation was successful, `pfnReallocation` must return an allocation with enough space for `size` bytes, and the contents of the original allocation from bytes zero to min(original size, new size) - 1 must be preserved in the returned allocation. If `size` is larger than the old size, the contents of the additional space are undefined. If satisfying these requirements involves creating a new allocation, then the old allocation should be freed.
L109: If `pOriginal` is `NULL`, then `pfnReallocation` must behave equivalently to a call to cite9†PFN_vkAllocationFunction with the same parameter values (without `pOriginal`).
L110: 
L111: If `size` is zero, then `pfnReallocation` must behave equivalently to a call to cite11†PFN_vkFreeFunction with the same `pUserData` parameter value, and `pMemory` equal to `pOriginal`.
L112: 
L113: If `pOriginal` is non-`NULL`, the implementation must ensure that `alignment` is equal to the `alignment` used to originally allocate `pOriginal`.
L114: If this function fails and `pOriginal` is non-`NULL` the application must not free the old allocation.
L115: 
L116: `pfnReallocation` must follow the same cite21†rules for return values as `PFN_vkAllocationFunction` .
L117: 
L118: The type of `pfnFree` is:
L119: 
L120:     `// Provided by VK_VERSION_1_0
L121:     typedef void (*PFN_vkFreeFunction)(
L122:         void*                                       pUserData,
L123:         void*                                       pMemory);`
L124:   * `pUserData` is the value specified for cite14†VkAllocationCallbacks ::`pUserData` in the allocator specified by the application.
L125: 
L126:   * `pMemory` is the allocation to be freed.
L127: 
L128: `pMemory` may be `NULL`, which the callback must handle safely. If `pMemory` is non-`NULL`, it must be a pointer previously allocated by `pfnAllocation` or `pfnReallocation`. The application should free this memory.
L129: The type of `pfnInternalAllocation` is:
L130: 
L131:     `// Provided by VK_VERSION_1_0
L132:     typedef void (*PFN_vkInternalAllocationNotification)(
L133:         void*                                       pUserData,
L134:         size_t                                      size,
L135:         VkInternalAllocationType                    allocationType,
L136:         VkSystemAllocationScope                     allocationScope);`
L137:   * `pUserData` is the value specified for cite14†VkAllocationCallbacks ::`pUserData` in the allocator specified by the application.
L138: 
L139:   * `size` is the requested size of an allocation.
L140: 
L141:   * `allocationType` is a cite22†VkInternalAllocationType value specifying the requested type of an allocation.
L142: 
L143:   * `allocationScope` is a cite15†VkSystemAllocationScope value specifying the allocation scope of the lifetime of the allocation, as described cite16†here .
L144: 
L145: This is a purely informational callback.
L146: The type of `pfnInternalFree` is:
L147: 
L148:     `// Provided by VK_VERSION_1_0
L149:     typedef void (*PFN_vkInternalFreeNotification)(
L150:         void*                                       pUserData,
L151:         size_t                                      size,
L152:         VkInternalAllocationType                    allocationType,
L153:         VkSystemAllocationScope                     allocationScope);`
L154:   * `pUserData` is the value specified for cite14†VkAllocationCallbacks ::`pUserData` in the allocator specified by the application.
L155: 
L156:   * `size` is the requested size of an allocation.
L157: 
L158:   * `allocationType` is a cite22†VkInternalAllocationType value specifying the requested type of an allocation.
L159: 
L160:   * `allocationScope` is a cite15†VkSystemAllocationScope value specifying the allocation scope of the lifetime of the allocation, as described cite16†here .
L161: Each allocation has an allocation scope defining its lifetime and which object it is associated with. Possible values passed to the `allocationScope` parameter of the callback functions specified by cite14†VkAllocationCallbacks , indicating the allocation scope, are:
L162: 
L163:     `// Provided by VK_VERSION_1_0
L164:     typedef enum VkSystemAllocationScope {
L165:         VK_SYSTEM_ALLOCATION_SCOPE_COMMAND = 0,
L166:         VK_SYSTEM_ALLOCATION_SCOPE_OBJECT = 1,
L167:         VK_SYSTEM_ALLOCATION_SCOPE_CACHE = 2,
L168:         VK_SYSTEM_ALLOCATION_SCOPE_DEVICE = 3,
L169:         VK_SYSTEM_ALLOCATION_SCOPE_INSTANCE = 4,
L170:     } VkSystemAllocationScope;`
L171:   * cite15†VK_SYSTEM_ALLOCATION_SCOPE_COMMAND specifies that the allocation is scoped to the duration of the Vulkan command.
L172: 
L173:   * cite15†VK_SYSTEM_ALLOCATION_SCOPE_OBJECT specifies that the allocation is scoped to the lifetime of the Vulkan object that is being created or used.
L174: 
L175:   * cite15†VK_SYSTEM_ALLOCATION_SCOPE_CACHE specifies that the allocation is scoped to the lifetime of a `VkPipelineCache` or `VkValidationCacheEXT` object.
L176:   * cite15†VK_SYSTEM_ALLOCATION_SCOPE_DEVICE specifies that the allocation is scoped to the lifetime of the Vulkan device.
L177: 
L178:   * cite15†VK_SYSTEM_ALLOCATION_SCOPE_INSTANCE specifies that the allocation is scoped to the lifetime of the Vulkan instance.
L179: Most Vulkan commands operate on a single object, or there is a sole object that is being created or manipulated. When an allocation uses an allocation scope of cite15†VK_SYSTEM_ALLOCATION_SCOPE_OBJECT or cite15†VK_SYSTEM_ALLOCATION_SCOPE_CACHE , the allocation is scoped to the object being created or manipulated.
L180: 
L181: When an implementation requires host memory, it will make callbacks to the application using the most specific allocator and allocation scope available:
L182:   * If an allocation is scoped to the duration of a command, the allocator will use the cite15†VK_SYSTEM_ALLOCATION_SCOPE_COMMAND allocation scope. The most specific allocator available is used: if the object being created or manipulated has an allocator, that object’s allocator will be used, else if the parent `VkDevice` has an allocator it will be used, else if the parent `VkInstance` has an allocator it will be used. Else,
L183:   * If an allocation is associated with a `VkValidationCacheEXT` or `VkPipelineCache` object, the allocator will use the cite15†VK_SYSTEM_ALLOCATION_SCOPE_CACHE allocation scope. The most specific allocator available is used (cache, else device, else instance). Else,
L184:   * If an allocation is scoped to the lifetime of an object, that object is being created or manipulated by the command, and that object’s type is not `VkDevice` or `VkInstance`, the allocator will use an allocation scope of cite15†VK_SYSTEM_ALLOCATION_SCOPE_OBJECT . The most specific allocator available is used (object, else device, else instance). Else,
L185:   * If an allocation is scoped to the lifetime of a device, the allocator will use an allocation scope of cite15†VK_SYSTEM_ALLOCATION_SCOPE_DEVICE . The most specific allocator available is used (device, else instance). Else,
L186: 
L187:   * If the allocation is scoped to the lifetime of an instance and the instance has an allocator, its allocator will be used with an allocation scope of cite15†VK_SYSTEM_ALLOCATION_SCOPE_INSTANCE .
L188:   * Otherwise an implementation will allocate memory through an alternative mechanism that is unspecified.
L189: 
L190: Objects that are allocated from pools do not specify their own allocator. When an implementation requires host memory for such an object, that memory is sourced from the object’s parent pool’s allocator.
L191: The application is not expected to handle allocating memory that is intended for execution by the host due to the complexities of differing security implementations across multiple platforms. The implementation will allocate such memory internally and invoke an application provided informational callback when these internal allocations are allocated and freed. Upon allocation of executable memory, `pfnInternalAllocation` will be called. Upon freeing executable memory, `pfnInternalFree` will be called.
L192: An implementation will only call an informational callback for executable memory allocations and frees.
L193: The `allocationType` parameter to the `pfnInternalAllocation` and `pfnInternalFree` functions may be one of the following values:
L194: 
L195:     `// Provided by VK_VERSION_1_0
L196:     typedef enum VkInternalAllocationType {
L197:         VK_INTERNAL_ALLOCATION_TYPE_EXECUTABLE = 0,
L198:     } VkInternalAllocationType;`
L199: 
L200:   * cite22†VK_INTERNAL_ALLOCATION_TYPE_EXECUTABLE specifies that the allocation is intended for execution by the host.
L201: An implementation must only make calls into an application-provided allocator during the execution of an API command. An implementation must only make calls into an application-provided allocator from the same thread that called the provoking API command. The implementation should not synchronize calls to any of the callbacks. If synchronization is needed, the callbacks must provide it themselves. The informational callbacks are subject to the same restrictions as the allocation callbacks.
L202: If an implementation intends to make calls through a `VkAllocationCallbacks` structure between the time a `vkCreate*` command returns and the time a corresponding `vkDestroy*` command begins, that implementation must save a copy of the allocator before the `vkCreate*` command returns. The callback functions and any data structures they rely upon must remain valid for the lifetime of the object they are associated with.
L203: If an allocator is provided to a `vkCreate*` command, a compatible allocator must be provided to the corresponding `vkDestroy*` command. Two `VkAllocationCallbacks` structures are compatible if memory allocated with `pfnAllocation` or `pfnReallocation` in each can be freed with `pfnReallocation` or `pfnFree` in the other. An allocator must not be provided to a `vkDestroy*` command if an allocator was not provided to the corresponding `vkCreate*` command.
L204: If a non-`NULL` allocator is used, the `pfnAllocation`, `pfnReallocation` and `pfnFree` members must be non-`NULL` and point to valid implementations of the callbacks. An application can choose to not provide informational callbacks by setting both `pfnInternalAllocation` and `pfnInternalFree` to `NULL`. `pfnInternalAllocation` and `pfnInternalFree` must either both be `NULL` or both be non-`NULL`.
L205: If `pfnAllocation` or `pfnReallocation` fail, the implementation may fail object creation and/or generate a cite19†VK_ERROR_OUT_OF_HOST_MEMORY error, as appropriate.
L206: 
L207: Allocation callbacks must not call any Vulkan commands.
L208: 
L209: The following sets of rules define when an implementation is permitted to call the allocator callbacks.
L210: 
L211: `pfnAllocation` or `pfnReallocation` may be called in the following situations:
L212: 
L213:   * Allocations scoped to a `VkDevice` or `VkInstance` may be allocated from any API command.
L214:   * Allocations scoped to a command may be allocated from any API command.
L215: 
L216:   * Allocations scoped to a `VkPipelineCache` may only be allocated from:
L217: 
L218:     * `vkCreatePipelineCache`
L219: 
L220:     * `vkMergePipelineCaches` for `dstCache`
L221: 
L222:     * `vkCreateGraphicsPipelines` for `pipelineCache`
L223: 
L224:     * `vkCreateComputePipelines` for `pipelineCache`
L225: 
L226:   * Allocations scoped to a `VkValidationCacheEXT` may only be allocated from:
L227: 
L228:     * `vkCreateValidationCacheEXT`
L229: 
L230:     * `vkMergeValidationCachesEXT` for `dstCache`
L231:     * `vkCreateShaderModule` for `validationCache` in cite23†VkShaderModuleValidationCacheCreateInfoEXT L232: 
L233:   * Allocations scoped to a `VkDescriptorPool` may only be allocated from:
L234: 
L235:     * any command that takes the pool as a direct argument
L236: 
L237:     * `vkAllocateDescriptorSets` for the `descriptorPool` member of its `pAllocateInfo` parameter
L238: 
L239:     * `vkCreateDescriptorPool`
L240: 
L241:   * Allocations scoped to a `VkCommandPool` may only be allocated from:
L242: 
L243:     * any command that takes the pool as a direct argument
L244:     * `vkCreateCommandPool`
L245: 
L246:     * `vkAllocateCommandBuffers` for the `commandPool` member of its `pAllocateInfo` parameter
L247: 
L248:     * any `vkCmd*` command whose `commandBuffer` was allocated from that `VkCommandPool`
L249: 
L250:   * Allocations scoped to any other object may only be allocated in that object’s `vkCreate*` command.
L251: 
L252: `pfnFree`, or `pfnReallocation` with zero `size`, may be called in the following situations:
L253: 
L254:   * Allocations scoped to a `VkDevice` or `VkInstance` may be freed from any API command.
L255:   * Allocations scoped to a command must be freed by any API command which allocates such memory.
L256: 
L257:   * Allocations scoped to a `VkPipelineCache` may be freed from `vkDestroyPipelineCache`.
L258: 
L259:   * Allocations scoped to a `VkValidationCacheEXT` may be freed from `vkDestroyValidationCacheEXT`.
L260: 
L261:   * Allocations scoped to a `VkDescriptorPool` may be freed from:
L262: 
L263:     * any command that takes the pool as a direct argument
L264: 
L265:   * Allocations scoped to a `VkCommandPool` may be freed from:
L266:     * any command that takes the pool as a direct argument
L267: 
L268:     * `vkResetCommandBuffer` whose `commandBuffer` was allocated from that `VkCommandPool`
L269: 
L270:   * Allocations scoped to any other object may be freed in that object’s `vkDestroy*` command.
L271: 
L272:   * Any command that allocates host memory may also free host memory of the same scope.
L273: ## Device Memory
L274: 
L275: Device memory is memory that is visible to the device — for example the contents of the image or buffer objects, which can be natively used by the device.
L276: ### Device Memory Properties
L277: 
L278: Memory properties of a physical device describe the memory heaps and memory types available.
L279: 
L280: To query memory properties, call:
L281:  | This functionality is superseded by cite24†vkGetPhysicalDeviceMemoryProperties2 . See cite25†Legacy Functionality for more information.
L282: 
L283:     `// Provided by VK_VERSION_1_0
L284:     void vkGetPhysicalDeviceMemoryProperties(
L285:         VkPhysicalDevice                            physicalDevice,
L286:         VkPhysicalDeviceMemoryProperties*           pMemoryProperties);`
L287: 
L288:   * `physicalDevice` is the handle to the device to query.
L289:   * `pMemoryProperties` is a pointer to a cite26†VkPhysicalDeviceMemoryProperties structure in which the properties are returned.
L290: 
L291: Valid Usage (Implicit)
L292: 
L293:   * VUID-vkGetPhysicalDeviceMemoryProperties-physicalDevice-parameter
L294: `physicalDevice` must be a valid cite27†VkPhysicalDevice handle
L295: 
L296:   * VUID-vkGetPhysicalDeviceMemoryProperties-pMemoryProperties-parameter
L297: `pMemoryProperties` must be a valid pointer to a cite26†VkPhysicalDeviceMemoryProperties structure
L298: The `VkPhysicalDeviceMemoryProperties` structure is defined as:
L299: 
L300:     `// Provided by VK_VERSION_1_0
L301:     typedef struct VkPhysicalDeviceMemoryProperties {
L302:         uint32_t        memoryTypeCount;
L303:         VkMemoryType    memoryTypes[VK_MAX_MEMORY_TYPES];
L304:         uint32_t        memoryHeapCount;
L305:         VkMemoryHeap    memoryHeaps[VK_MAX_MEMORY_HEAPS];
L306:     } VkPhysicalDeviceMemoryProperties;`
L307: 
L308:   * `memoryTypeCount` is the number of valid elements in the `memoryTypes` array.

L314: The `VkPhysicalDeviceMemoryProperties` structure describes a number of memory heaps as well as a number of memory types that can be used to access memory allocated in those heaps. every list of numbers, `F(list)` returns the same numbers in ascending order".
Models are then guaranteed to respond with bug-free code, since Bend will demand
that they provide an actual proof.

> We envision that "law-driven development" will eventually become the way humans
> use AI to write and maintain large codebases, as it is the perfect middle point
> between having to code everything manually (laborious) and letting AI do it all
> via prompts without auditing a line of code (error/ambiguity-prone, unsecure).

By convention, a project keeps its laws in two files at its root. `LAWS.bend`
imports the code and states the laws, each an open claim: the human writes it,
the AI does not touch it. `PROOF.bend` imports `LAWS.bend` and proves each law
with a def of the same name (`law sorted` is proven by `def Laws.sorted`): the
AI writes it, along with the code. `bend PROOF.bend` is the gate: it prints
SOME PROOFS FAIL while any law is open or false, and ALL PROOFS CHECK once every
law holds.
bend refuses a `PROOF.bend` that sits beside a `LAWS.bend` without importing it.

`bend PROOF.bend --verdict` checks the proofs a second time, with a small kernel
that has a proof in Lean: it prints ALL PROOFS CHECK only when every def outside
Base is a valid proof, which bend2 and the kernel both accept, and which relies
on no `@unsafe` or foreign code. `-o PROOF.bendtt` writes the translation the
kernel reads; the translation has no proof, so read it to confirm a law.

Bend has no tactics: a proposition is a type, and a proof is a def of that type.
`{a == b : T}` is an equality; `{==}` proves it when both sides compute to the
same term. Matching refines the goal in each case, a recursive call is the
induction hypothesis, and `%e : P` rewrites with `e : {a == b : T}`: `P` is the
goal with `_` marking `b`, and the goal becomes `P` with `a` there. `exs y: T`
in a law asks for a witness, returned as `(y, proof)`. A failed step prints the
expected and observed terms; `?name` prints the goal, `?TODO` leaves it open,
and a law with no def is an open claim.

Since types are terms, a def may return a `Type`, like `def IsEven(n: Nat) ->
Type:`, which is all dependent types are. A `match e:` with no cases closes a
branch where `e : Empty`. To refute a clash like `e : {1n == 0n : Nat}`, rewrite
it through a motive `disc(_)`, where `disc` sends `0n` to `Empty` and `1n+p` to
`Unit`, and answer `Unit{}`. `{a != b : T}` is `{a == b : T} -> Empty`, and
`Equal.sym`, `Equal.trans` and `Equal.cong` are in Base.

### IO and Concurrency

Effects live in the `IO` type and are sequenced with `do` blocks:

```python
import Base

def greet(name: String) -> IO(String):
  do IO<String>:
    IO.sleep(1000)             # a step
    return "Hello, " ++ name   # return: wraps a pure value

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    name : String <- IO.try(String, IO.get_env("USER")) # <-: binds a result
    chan : Chan(String) <- IO.fork(String, greet(name)) # runs concurrently
    IO.print("Waiting...")
    text : String <- IO.join(String, chan)
    IO.print(text)
```

Every bind is annotated, and `x : T = v` binds a pure value in the middle of a
block. A fallible effect answers `Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, A>`: `IO.try`
unwraps it or exits with the error, and `IO.die` exits with your own. `IO.args`
answers the command line, less the runtime's own options (a `--` ends them):
its head is the program as invoked, like C's `argv[0]`. A handle (`File`,
`Socket`, `Window`) is an affine, opaque value, so every effect on one hands it
back beside its result, and no program can forge or reuse one.

`TCP.listen(host, port)` and `UDP.bind(host, port)` bind the IPv4 literal
`host`: `"127.0.0.1"` serves this machine only, `"0.0.0.0"` every interface.
A bad address or a port above 65535 fails with `EINVAL`.

`Process.run(program, args, input, max_output, timeout_ms)` starts an
executable directly, with literal arguments rather than a shell. It inherits
the current directory and environment, writes UTF-8 `input` to its stdin, and
answers `Done{(status, (stdout, stderr))}` even when the exit status is not
zero. Both limits must be positive; failure to start, a timeout, or stdout
and stderr exceeding `max_output` bytes together answer `Fail`. The call
returns once the child exits and stdout and stderr close, so a descendant
holding a pipe open delays it, up to the timeout. Timeouts do not kill
descendants.
A native build runs the child on an IO helper thread; the JavaScript lane
blocks while the child runs. On Linux, native builds need glibc 2.34 or newer
to close inherited descriptors. It does not sandbox the child: callers must
whether a command is trusted before executing it.

A Bend program is a set of computations interleaved by one event loop, as in
Node.js: one at a time, each runs its pure code, on every core through its
[parallel calls](#parallelism), up to its next effect, and one that waits on a
socket, a sleep or a channel steps aside for the others. `IO.fork` starts a
computation and returns the channel its result will arrive on; `IO.join` waits
for it. Underneath are `IO.spawn`, `Chan.new`, `Chan.send`, `Chan.recv` and
`Chan.close`. `IO.within(A, ms, act)` races `act` against a deadline and answers
`None{}` if the deadline wins; the loser is not cancelled. The program ends when
every computation is done, or reports a deadlock when the remaining ones all
wait.

Every effect in Base is a def whose body is `import "./x.js"` plus a `.c` twin,
implemented by a host function named after the def, lowercased, dots to
underscores. You can add your own effects the same way. Only the event loop runs
them, so proofs, termination and the GPU never touch host code. In the other
direction, a JS file may `import Game from "./game.bend"` (with `bend2/main.ts`
preloaded), or from the `./game.mjs` that `-o game.mjs` writes, and call every
non-IO def, with constructors as `{$: "Name", field: value}` and `Nat` as a
number. A value crosses without a copy: an `Array`
argument is the caller's own array, updated in place, so copy it first if you
keep it.

### Monads

The `do` notation works for any monad, not just IO.

```python
import Base

def add_strs(a: String, b: String) -> Maybe<&2, U32>:
  do Maybe<&2, U32>:
    x : U32 <- U32.read(a) # a None here ends the block with None
    y : U32 <- U32.read(b)
    return (x + y : U32)
```

### IO and Concurrency

Effects live in the `IO` type and are sequenced with `do` blocks:

```python
import Base

def greet(name: String) -> IO(String):
  do IO<String>:
    IO.sleep(1000)             # a step
    return "Hello, " ++ name   # return: wraps a pure value

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    name : String <- IO.try(String, IO.get_env("USER")) # <-: binds a result
    chan : Chan(String) <- IO.fork(String, greet(name)) # runs concurrently
    IO.print("Waiting...")
    text : String <- IO.join(String, chan)
    IO.print(text)
```

block. A fallible effect answers `Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, A>`: `IO.try`
unwraps it or exits with the error, and `IO.die` exits with your own. `IO.args`
answers the command line, less the runtime's own options (a `--` ends them):
its head is the program as invoked, like C's `argv[0]`. A handle (`File`,
`Socket`, `Window`) is an affine, opaque value, so every effect on one hands it
back beside its result, and no program can forge or reuse one.

executable directly, with literal arguments rather than a shell. It inherits

returns once the child exits and stdout and stderr close, so a descendant
holding a pipe open delays it, up to the timeout. Timeouts do not kill
descendants.

L2: # vkMapMemory(3)
L3: 
L4: ## Name
L5: 
L6: vkMapMemory - Map a memory object into application address space
L7: ## C Specification
L8: To retrieve a host virtual address pointer to a region of a mappable memory object, call:
L9: 
L10:     `// Provided by VK_VERSION_1_0
L11:     VkResult vkMapMemory(
L12:         VkDevice                                    device,
L13:         VkDeviceMemory                              memory,
L14:         VkDeviceSize                                offset,
L15:         VkDeviceSize                                size,
L16:         VkMemoryMapFlags                            flags,
L17:         void**                                      ppData);`
L18: ## Parameters
L19: 
L20:   * `device` is the logical device that owns the memory.
L21: 
L22:   * `memory` is the cite1†VkDeviceMemory object to be mapped.
L23: 
L24:   * `offset` is a zero-based byte offset from the beginning of the memory object.
L25: 
L26:   * `size` is the size of the memory range to map, or cite2†VK_WHOLE_SIZE to map from `offset` to the end of the allocation.
L27: 
L28:   * `flags` is a bitmask of cite3†VkMemoryMapFlagBits specifying additional parameters of the memory map operation.
L29:   * `ppData` is a pointer to a `void*` variable in which a host-accessible pointer to the beginning of the mapped range is returned. The value of the returned pointer minus `offset` must be aligned to cite4†VkPhysicalDeviceLimits ::`minMemoryMapAlignment`.
L30: ## Description
L31: 
L32: After a successful call to `vkMapMemory` the memory object `memory` is considered to be currently host mapped.
L33: 
L34:  | It is an application error to call `vkMapMemory` on a memory object that is already host mapped.
L35:  | `vkMapMemory` will fail if the implementation is unable to allocate an appropriately sized contiguous virtual address range, e.g. due to virtual address space fragmentation or platform limits. In such cases, `vkMapMemory` must return cite5†VK_ERROR_MEMORY_MAP_FAILED . The application can improve the likelihood of success by reducing the size of the mapped range and/or removing unneeded mappings using cite6†vkUnmapMemory .
L36: `vkMapMemory` does not check whether the device memory is currently in use before returning the host-accessible pointer. The application must guarantee that any previously submitted command that writes to this range has completed before the host reads from or writes to that range, and that any previously submitted command that reads from that range has completed before the host writes to that region (see cite7†here for details on fulfilling such a guarantee).
L37: If the device memory was allocated without the cite8†VK_MEMORY_PROPERTY_HOST_COHERENT_BIT set, these guarantees must be made for an extended range: the application must round down the start of the range to the nearest multiple of cite4†VkPhysicalDeviceLimits ::`nonCoherentAtomSize`, and round the end of the range up to the nearest multiple of cite4†VkPhysicalDeviceLimits ::`nonCoherentAtomSize`.
L38: While a range of device memory is host mapped, the application is responsible for synchronizing both device and host access to that memory range.
L39: 
L40:  | It is important for the application developer to become meticulously familiar with all of the mechanisms described in the chapter on cite9†Synchronization and Cache Control as they are crucial to maintaining memory access ordering.
L41: 
L42: Calling `vkMapMemory` is equivalent to calling cite10†vkMapMemory2 with an empty `pNext` chain.
L43: 
L44: Valid Usage
L45:   * VUID-vkMapMemory-memory-00678
L46: `memory` must not be currently host mapped
L47: 
L48:   * VUID-vkMapMemory-offset-00679
L49: `offset` must be less than the size of `memory`
L50: 
L51:   * VUID-vkMapMemory-size-00680
L52: If `size` is not equal to cite2†VK_WHOLE_SIZE , `size` must be greater than `0`
L53: 
L54:   * VUID-vkMapMemory-size-00681
L55: If `size` is not equal to cite2†VK_WHOLE_SIZE , `size` must be less than or equal to the size of the `memory` minus `offset`
L56:   * VUID-vkMapMemory-memory-00682
L57: `memory` must have been created with a memory type that reports cite8†VK_MEMORY_PROPERTY_HOST_VISIBLE_BIT L58: 
L59:   * VUID-vkMapMemory-memory-00683
L60: `memory` must not have been allocated with multiple instances
L61: 
L62:   * VUID-vkMapMemory-flags-09568
L63: cite3†VK_MEMORY_MAP_PLACED_BIT_EXT must not be set in `flags`
L64: 
L65: Valid Usage (Implicit)
L66: 
L67:   * VUID-vkMapMemory-device-parameter
L68: `device` must be a valid cite11†VkDevice handle
L69:   * VUID-vkMapMemory-memory-parameter
L70: `memory` must be a valid cite1†VkDeviceMemory handle
L71: 
L72:   * VUID-vkMapMemory-flags-parameter
L73: If `flags` is not `0`, `flags` must be a valid combination of cite3†VkMemoryMapFlagBits values
L74: 
L75:   * VUID-vkMapMemory-ppData-parameter
L76: `ppData` must be a valid pointer to a pointer value
L77: 
L78:   * VUID-vkMapMemory-memory-parent
L79: `memory` must have been created, allocated, or retrieved from `device`
L80: 
L81: Host Synchronization
L82: 
L83:   * Host access to `memory` must be externally synchronized

L2: # vkFlushMappedMemoryRanges(3)
L3: 
L4: ## Name
L5: 
L6: vkFlushMappedMemoryRanges - Flush mapped memory ranges
L7: 
L8: ## C Specification
L9: 
L10: To flush ranges of non-coherent memory from the host caches, call:
L11: 
L12:     `// Provided by VK_VERSION_1_0
L13:     VkResult vkFlushMappedMemoryRanges(
L14:         VkDevice                                    device,
L15:         uint32_t                                    memoryRangeCount,
L16:         const VkMappedMemoryRange*                  pMemoryRanges);`
L17: ## Parameters
L18: 
L19:   * `device` is the logical device that owns the memory ranges.
L20: 
L21:   * `memoryRangeCount` is the length of the `pMemoryRanges` array.
L22: 
L23:   * `pMemoryRanges` is a pointer to an array of cite1†VkMappedMemoryRange structures describing the memory ranges to flush.
L24: ## Description
L25: 
L26: `vkFlushMappedMemoryRanges` guarantees that host writes to the memory ranges described by `pMemoryRanges` are made available to the host memory domain, such that they can be made available to the device memory domain via cite2†memory domain operations using the cite3†VK_ACCESS_HOST_WRITE_BIT cite4†access type .
L27: 
L28: The first cite5†synchronization scope includes all host operations that happened-before it, as defined by the host memory model.
L29:  | Some systems allow writes that do not directly integrate with the host memory model; these have to be synchronized by the application manually. One example of this is non-temporal store instructions on x86; to ensure these happen-before submission, applications should call `_mm_sfence()`.
L30: 
L31: The second cite5†synchronization scope is empty.
L32: 
L33: The first cite6†access scope includes host writes to the specified memory ranges.
L34:  | When a host write to a memory location is made available in this way, each whole aligned set of cite7†`nonCoherentAtomSize` bytes that the memory location exists in will also be made available as if they were written by the host. For example, with a `nonCoherentAtomSize` of 128, if an application writes to the first byte of a memory object via a host mapping, the first 128 bytes of the memory object will be made available by this command.
L35: While the value of the following 127 bytes will be unchanged, this does count as an access for the purpose of synchronization, so care must be taken to avoid data races.
L36: The second cite6†access scope is empty.
L37: 
L38: Unmapping non-coherent memory does not implicitly flush the host mapped memory, and host writes that have not been flushed may not ever be visible to the device. However, implementations must ensure that writes that have not been flushed do not become visible to any other memory.
L39:  | The above guarantee avoids a potential memory corruption in scenarios where host writes to a mapped memory object have not been flushed before the memory is unmapped (or freed), and the virtual address range is subsequently reused for a different mapping (or memory allocation).
L40: 
L41: Valid Usage (Implicit)
L42: 
L43:   * VUID-vkFlushMappedMemoryRanges-device-parameter
L44: `device` must be a valid cite8†VkDevice handle
L45:   * VUID-vkFlushMappedMemoryRanges-pMemoryRanges-parameter
L46: `pMemoryRanges` must be a valid pointer to an array of `memoryRangeCount` valid cite1†VkMappedMemoryRange structures
L47: 
L48:   * VUID-vkFlushMappedMemoryRanges-memoryRangeCount-arraylength
L49: `memoryRangeCount` must be greater than `0`

# Effects in Bend

An AI wrote this text from the runtime's source (`bend2/comp.ts` and
`bend2/effs/`). A human will revise it later. Report anything wrong on
GitHub.

## An effect def

An effect is a def of type `IO(R)` whose body is two imports:

```python
def Clock.now() -> IO(U32):
  import "./clock.c"
  import "./clock.js"
```

Each file registers the effect under its def with `io_eff(CID(Clock.now),
..)`. The `.c` file serves `bend x.bend -o x`; the `.js` file
serves `bend x.bend -o x.js` and `bend x.bend`. Every effect in Base is
built this way: `bend2/effs/*.c` and `*.js` are the reference.

## The C side

The compiler splices your `.c` into the program's C source after the
runtime, so every runtime symbol is in scope. Define the effect and
register it in a constructor:

```c
Term clock_now_run(Env e, Term* f, IoWork* w);

static void __attribute__((constructor)) clock_now_use(void) {
  io_eff(CID(Clock.now), clock_now_run);
}
```

`CID(Name)` is the C id of a constructor or of an effect def: the compiler
replaces it with the name's own id, reading `Name` in the effect's
namespace first (the file that declares the def), then in Base's, as the
def's body would. A constructor the program does not use has no id, so
`#ifdef CID(Name)` tests for it. `FID(name)` is a def's function id the
same way. `f` holds the def's arguments in order: a `U32` is the word
(`(u32)f[0]`), a `String` is taken with `io_cstr(e, f[0], &len)` (a
`malloc`ed copy you free), a handle with `io_hand_v(f[0])`. The loop
calls the effect at once; an effect that waits (for a handle, or for time)
parks itself, as below.

The effect returns a Term: a `U32` is `(Term)n`, `Unit` is
`term_pak(CID(Unit), 0)`, a `String` is `io_str(e, p, n)`, a two-field
constructor is `io_node(e, CID(K), a, b)`. A `Result` is `io_done(e, v)`
or `io_fail(e, code, text)` (`text` NULL prints `strerror(code)`).
`io_sys_end(w, n)` stores `errno` in `w->code` when a call fails.

A handle is a descriptor or pointer packed in one word by `io_hand(v)`. Its
type must be one of Base's handle laws (`File`, `Socket`, ...): a user
handle type is a WONTFIX entry for now, see `WONTFIX.txt`. An effect on a
handle hands it back beside its result: `io_tup(e, io_hand(h), r)`, also
on failure.

Blocking work leaves the loop in two ways. `io_work(w, call, pack)` runs
`call(w)` on a helper thread, then `pack(e, w)` on the loop; `pack`'s value
is the answer. `call` has no `Env`: it may only touch `w`.
`io_wait_on(w, fd, POLLIN, 0, more)` parks until `fd` is ready (`POLLIN` or
`POLLOUT`), then runs `more(e, w)` on the loop; `more` may call
`io_wait_on` again. Both return `IO_PARK`, which the effect returns.
Replace `0` with an absolute `io_tick()` deadline to also wake on time;
with no events (`io_wait_on(w, 0, 0, deadline, more)`) it waits on time
alone, as `sleep.c` does. An effect that can meet a steady backlog (an
accept, a datagram recv) parks before its first try, as `tcp_accept.c`
does: one that answers at once never lets the loop poll, so the backlog
would starve its timers.

`w` is the effect's scratch space: `hand`, `made`, `size`, `data`, `text`,
`code`, and `word` until it parks (`io_wait_on` keeps its fd there). The
runtime owns `w` and `f`. The effect owns `w->data`:
allocate it in the run function and free it in `pack`. In `bend2/effs/`,
`file_read.c` is the pattern for `io_work` and `tcp_recv.c` for `io_wait_on`.

## The JS side

The `.js` file is a plain script, run once in a closure of its own, that
registers the effect: `io_eff(CID(Clock.now), clock_now)`. The effect
takes the def's arguments as JS values: a `U32` is a number, a `Nat` a
number, a `String` a string, a constructor
`{$: CID(Name), field: value}`, a handle its host value (a descriptor).
`CID(Name)` is the constructor's tag, read as on the C side. It returns
the answer the same way: `io_done(v)`, `io_fail(code)`,
`io_tup(handle, result)`, `{$: CID(Unit)}`. A `Nat` answer that is not a
whole number from 0 to 2^53 stops the run; a `Nat` inside an answer goes
unchecked, so the host keeps it in that range.

A blocking effect takes one more argument, `k`, and parks with
`io_park_on(fd, out, k, more)`: it returns `undefined`, and the loop calls
`more()` when `fd` is ready; `more` answers the value, or `undefined` to
park again. Add an absolute `performance.now()` deadline as a fifth
argument to also wake on time; with no fd
(`io_park_on(undefined, false, k, more, deadline)`) it waits on time
alone, as `sleep.js` does. An effect that can meet a steady backlog
parks before its first try, as on the C side. `io_sys()` is `libc` through `bun:ffi`
(`read`, `recv`, `select`, `errno`); `tcp_accept.js` shows the full shape.

## A complete example

`main.bend`:

```python
import Base

def Clock.now() -> IO(U32):
  import "./clock.c"
  import "./clock.js"

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    t : U32 <- Clock.now()
    IO.print("ms since boot: " ++ U32.show(t))
```

`clock.c`:

```c
Term clock_now_run(Env e, Term* f, IoWork* w) {
  return (Term)(uint32_t)(io_tick() / 1000000ull);
}

static void __attribute__((constructor)) clock_now_use(void) {
  io_eff(CID(Clock.now), clock_now_run);
}
```

`clock.js`:

```js
function clock_now() {
  return Math.floor(performance.now()) >>> 0;
}

io_eff(CID(Clock.now), clock_now);
```

`bend main.bend -o main && ./main` prints a line; so do `bend main.bend -o
main.js && bun main.js` and `bend main.bend`. The output name must not be
one of the effect's files.

## Compatibility

The C side tracks the exact compiler version: the names above are the
runtime's internals, and a release may rename any of them. There is no ABI
promise. Rebuild your effects with every update.

`CID(Name)` is the constructor's tag, read as on the C side. It returns
the answer the same way: `io_done(v)`, `io_fail(code)`,
`io_tup(handle, result)`, `{$: CID(Unit)}`. A `Nat` answer that is not a
whole number from 0 to 2^53 stops the run; a `Nat` inside an answer goes
unchecked, so the host keeps it in that range.

A blocking effect takes one more argument, `k`, and parks with
`io_park_on(fd, out, k, more)`: it returns `undefined`, and the loop calls
`more()` when `fd` is ready; `more` answers the value, or `undefined` to
park again. Add an absolute `performance.now()` deadline as a fifth
argument to also wake on time; with no fd
(`io_park_on(undefined, false, k, more, deadline)`) it waits on time
alone, as `sleep.js` does. An effect that can meet a steady backlog
parks before its first try, as on the C side. `io_sys()` is `libc` through `bun:ffi`
(`read`, `recv`, `select`, `errno`); `tcp_accept.js` shows the full shape.

## A complete example

`main.bend`:

```python
import Base

def Clock.now() -> IO(U32):
  import "./clock.c"
  import "./clock.js"

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    t : U32 <- Clock.now()
    IO.print("ms since boot: " ++ U32.show(t))
```

`clock.c`:

```c
Term clock_now_run(Env e, Term* f, IoWork* w) {
  return (Term)(uint32_t)(io_tick() / 1000000ull);
}

static void __attribute__((constructor)) clock_now_use(void) {
  io_eff(CID(Clock.now), clock_now_run);
}
```

`clock.js`:

```js
function clock_now() {
  return Math.floor(performance.now()) >>> 0;
}

io_eff(CID(Clock.now), clock_now);
```

`bend main.bend -o main && ./main` prints a line; so do `bend main.bend -o
main.js && bun main.js` and `bend main.bend`. The output name must not be
one of the effect's files.

## Compatibility

The C side tracks the exact compiler version: the names above are the
runtime's internals, and a release may rename any of them. There is no ABI
promise. Rebuild your effects with every update.

```python
# Discovery: with_entry loads, runs this callback, and closes on Done or Fail.
def discover(+e: V.Entry) -> V.Vk<Unit>:
  do V.Vk<Unit>:
    i : V.Instance <- V.Entry.create_instance(e, V.InstanceConfig.headless())

def buffer_bytes(+i: V.Instance, +p: V.PhysicalDevice) -> V.Vk<List<U32>>:
  do V.Vk<List<U32>>:
    d : V.Device <- V.Instance.create_device(i, p, V.DeviceConfig.one_queue(0))

    V.Error.report_result(result)
```

An ash-like starting point needs real loader/instance/device dispatch and independently useful Vulkan operations. ## Shape

Sketch notation groups similar constructors/signatures for readability; implementation uses ordinary Bend declarations and explicit quantity parameters.

```python
# Each of these is Data: Entry{key: W.U64}, Instance{key: W.U64}, Device{key: W.U64},
# PhysicalDevice{key: W.U64}, Buffer{key: W.U64}, DeviceMemory{key: W.U64}.
type Error is Data:
  Vulkan{command: String, code_bits: U32}  # exact signed VkResult bit pattern
  Loader{code: U32, message: String}
  InvalidHandle{operation: String}
  InvalidArgument{message: String}
  Unsupported{feature: String}
  EnumerationUnstable{}
  Cleanup{primary: Maybe<Error>, failures: List<Error>}
# InstanceConfig{application_name:String, api_version:U32, layers:List<String>, extensions:List<String>}
# DeviceConfig{queues:List<QueueRequest>, extensions:List<String>}; QueueRequest{family:U32, priorities:List<F32>}
# BufferConfig{size:W.U64, usage:U32}; initially exclusive sharing, zero create flags.
# MemoryAllocateInfo{size:W.U64, memory_type_index:U32}
# MemoryRequirements{size:W.U64, alignment:W.U64, memory_type_bits:U32}
# MemoryProperties includes U64 heap sizes; PhysicalDeviceInfo includes name/type/API and queue families.
def Entry.load() -> IO(Result<&1,&1,U32 & String,Entry>):
  import "./native.c"
  import "./native.js"

# Entry.create_instance(Entry, InstanceConfig) -> Vk<Instance>
# Instance.enumerate_physical_devices(Instance) -> Vk<List<PhysicalDevice>>
# Instance.describe_all(Instance, List<PhysicalDevice>) -> Vk<List<PhysicalDeviceInfo>>
# Instance.memory_properties(Instance, PhysicalDevice) -> Vk<MemoryProperties>
# Instance.create_device(Instance, PhysicalDevice, DeviceConfig) -> Vk<Device>
# Device.{create_buffer,buffer_requirements,allocate_memory,bind_buffer_memory}: see usage
# Device.write_memory(Device, DeviceMemory, W.U64, List<U32>) -> Vk<Unit>
# Device.read_memory(Device, DeviceMemory, W.U64, W.U64) -> Vk<List<U32>>
# Device.destroy_buffer(Device, Buffer), free_memory(Device, DeviceMemory), destroy(Device) -> Vk<Unit>
# Instance.destroy(Instance), Entry.close(Entry) -> Vk<Unit>
# Pure MemoryType.select(MemoryRequirements, MemoryProperties, U32) -> Maybe<U32>
```

`List<U32>` is a byte sequence here: validate each element <=255, never silently truncate. All Vulkan byte sizes, offsets, requirements, alignment and heap sizes use collections U64. C reconstructs `((uint64_t)hi << 32) | lo`; only allocation/copy lengths are checked against SIZE_MAX and practical return-size limits. Pure unsigned comparison and overflow-safe bounds use both limbs, never collections `le_signed`.

Native Entry rows own a dlopen handle and global PFNs; Instance rows own VkInstance plus instance PFNs; Device rows own VkDevice plus device PFNs. Resolve global functions through vkGetInstanceProcAddr(NULL,...), instance functions through the created instance, and device functions through vkGetDeviceProcAddr. Required missing PFNs fail loading; absent vkEnumerateInstanceVersion means Vulkan 1.0. Tables remain alive until their descendants are gone. This follows ash’s three dispatch levels ([ash Entry](https://docs.rs/ash/latest/ash/struct.Entry.html), [Khronos dispatch](https://docs.vulkan.org/refpages/latest/refpages/source/vkGetInstanceProcAddr.html)).

The native registry assigns a globally unique slot/generation U64 to every row, recording kind, parent, actual Vulkan handle and cleanup state. Slots never reuse a generation after wrap: retire them. Validate constructor layout, key, generation, kind, live ancestor chain and common device/instance before touching native objects. Never cast user U64 bits to VkInstance/VkDevice, a pointer, a PFN or a mapped address. An existing ID is a reference, not an unforgeable security capability; copying it aliases one checked object. Per boundary-discipline, all validation lives at effects; per model-the-domain, native rows represent bound/mapped/freed states explicitly.

Only the Bend event loop executes these native Vulkan effects; no IO.fork or parallel Bend calls submit Vulkan work. The registry is consequently a single writer, with ownership lists per Entry rather than one global teardown list. Independent pure preparation, device ranking, byte generation and result comparisons can use balanced Bend parallel calls. Data handle views avoid fictitious affine/RAII guarantees: dropping a constructor cannot release C allocations; with_entry is the default ownership boundary.

Use the normal constructor ABI (`io_node`, `io_tup`, U64 limbs), never `io_hand` for these types. Register effects with `io_eff` using the installed compiler ABI. `io_done` builds successful Result values; domain Fail constructors contain Error, while `io_fail` is appropriate for Entry.load's specified U32/String bootstrap error. `io_cstr` buffers and temporary marshalled arrays have explicit C frees. C owns temporary Vk structs, sets sType/pNext/counts and keeps strings/arrays alive through each call. JS registers matching effects and returns an explicit native-only error. Compile native executables for integration checks.

## Cleanup and observable behavior

Every successful creation enters its owner ledger before publishing the ID; failure after native creation destroys that object before returning. Explicit child destruction invalidates the ID, repeated close succeeds for an already retired matching ID, and forged/unrelated IDs fail. Destroying a parent with live children reports InvalidArgument; Entry.close is the documented cascading exception. Track binding references: free_memory refuses live bound buffers, and failed binding commits no relationship.
Scope close unmaps any outstanding mapping, destroys buffers, frees memory, destroys devices and instances, then dlcloses Entry; use dependency order, not arbitrary reverse creation order. Preserve the callback's error and collect cleanup failures in Cleanup. Entry.close runs even on Vk Fail, but cannot promise cleanup after process termination or IO.die; examples avoid IO.try inside owned scopes. Parent teardown cannot unload a child's PFNs.
Read/write are convenience operations on already bound host-visible allocations, not exported map pointers: map the whole allocation, validate the requested subrange, copy bytes and unmap on every exit. Noncoherent writes flush and reads invalidate a whole-allocation range while mapped; no concurrent GPU work is supported initially. This hides cache/alignment/pointer handling behind two operations ([mapping rules](https://docs.vulkan.org/refpages/latest/refpages/source/vkMapMemory.html), [flush rules](https://docs.vulkan.org/refpages/latest/refpages/source/vkFlushMappedMemoryRanges.html)).
Enumeration loops use count/query/retry with bounded native retries for VK_INCOMPLETE; positive Vulkan statuses are interpreted by command, never treated as generic success. Preserve raw VkResult bits and command names without inventing a Vulkan error for wrapper validation. Reject unsupported requested versions/extensions/configuration before publishing dispatch objects.

## Module layout and generated path

`src/vulkan.bend` is the public import; `src/vk_types.bend` owns configs/errors/pure selection; `src/dispatch.bend` owns effects and scope helpers; `src/native.c`/`.js` own marshalling/registry/dispatch. Existing `deps/bend-collections` supplies U64. `examples/discover.bend` and `examples/buffer_roundtrip.bend` exercise separate reusable calls. A native runtime compatibility smoke program precedes implementation.
`tools/generate.py` consumes pinned Khronos vk.xml plus a small support manifest and deterministically emits enums, flags, version helpers and PFN table/load lists into `src/generated/`; retain source revision and licenses. Emit only supported commands, fail generation on unknown field shapes, and report unsupported surface explicitly. Keep hand-written memory/config marshalling until the generator has supported pointer-length/lifetime rules; a blanket registry translator is not the first milestone.
`LAWS.bend` specifies unsigned U64 comparison/bounds, memory-type selection soundness and selected failure cases; `PROOF.bend` imports it and proves the pure implementation. Native ABI, Vulkan state and driver behavior remain integration obligations. Before commit run `bend PROOF.bend`, generation freshness, native discovery and 16-byte allocate/bind/write/read/assert/cleanup. Include limb preservation above 2^32 without allocating gigabytes, forged/stale/wrong-parent IDs, injected partial-create failure and zero live registry rows. Validation layers, when installed, must report no ownership/memory errors; software Vulkan is an acceptable explicit integration backend, no available ICD is an explicit unmet prerequisite.

## Tradeoffs accepted and alternatives considered

We accept runtime-checked Data references and a scoped native ledger for concise ash-like calls and reliable error cleanup; callers still choose queues, flags, memory types and lifetimes. The interface hides loader ABI, object validation and marshalling without reducing Vulkan to one demonstration function.
Raw U64 handles/pointers expose invalid-pointer dereferences to ordinary Bend construction; rejected. Affine wrappers without a native ledger expose failure-path leaks and still allow forged constructors; rejected. One opaque GPU/session with only upload/download hides useful requirements/allocation/dispatch choices; rejected for insufficiently reusable capability. Generating the complete Vulkan API immediately hides neither pointer lifetimes nor extension constraints; rejected for an unauditable initial boundary.

## Open questions and next implementation step

Should later command submission retain this checked-reference API or introduce separate affine recording/queue capabilities? Defer until submission exists; current scope needs no user decision. First implement Entry.load/close plus one constructor/U64/error ABI smoke executable, then the dependency-ordered native ledger and discovery-to-memory roundtrip. Synthesis decision belongs to the parent design comparison.

```python
    V.Vk.print(V.PhysicalDeviceInfo.show_all(infos))

# Allocation: keep Vulkan's requirements/type-selection/allocation/binding visible.
def buffer_bytes(+i: V.Instance, +p: V.PhysicalDevice) -> V.Vk<List<U32>>:
  do V.Vk<List<U32>>:
    d : V.Device <- V.Instance.create_device(i, p, V.DeviceConfig.one_queue(0))
    b : V.Buffer <- V.Device.create_buffer(d, V.BufferConfig{W.of_u32(16), V.TRANSFER_SRC})
    req : V.MemoryRequirements <- V.Device.buffer_requirements(d, b)
    props : V.MemoryProperties <- V.Instance.memory_properties(i, p)
    mt : U32 <- V.Vk.require_memory_type(req, props, V.HOST_VISIBLE)
    m : V.DeviceMemory <- V.Device.allocate_memory(d, V.MemoryAllocateInfo{req.size, mt})
    V.Device.bind_buffer_memory(d, b, m, W.zero())
    V.Device.write_memory(d, m, W.zero(), [1, 2, 3, 4])
    V.Device.read_memory(d, m, W.zero(), W.of_u32(4))

# Application boundary: errors remain inspectable; scope cleanup already ran.
def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    result : Result<&1,&1,V.Error,Unit> <- V.Vk.with_entry(Unit, discover)
    V.Error.report_result(result)
```
The actual roundtrip example first queries queue families and selects a supported nonempty family; `one_queue(0)` above is an explicit caller choice, checked against the selected device. Scope exit releases the sample's resources; long-lived applications also have explicit destroy/free operations.

## Problem

An ash-like starting point needs real loader/instance/device dispatch and independently useful Vulkan operations. Bend 2.0.37 cannot declare custom opaque foreign handles, and ordinary constructors are forgeable. Therefore constructors carry checked references, while native code owns all pointers, dispatch tables, and object lifetimes. Initial support is Linux/headless Vulkan 1.0 discovery, device creation, buffers and host-visible memory; no renderer, swapchains, command submission, shader pipelines, general pNext chains, callbacks, or allocator callbacks.

## Shape

Sketch notation groups similar constructors/signatures for readability; implementation uses ordinary Bend declarations and explicit quantity parameters.
```python
# Import deps/bend-collections/src/math/u64.bend; use its actual U64, never a replacement.
# Each of these is Data: Entry{key: W.U64}, Instance{key: W.U64}, Device{key: W.U64},
# PhysicalDevice{key: W.U64}, Buffer{key: W.U64}, DeviceMemory{key: W.U64}.
type Error is Data:
  Vulkan{command: String, code_bits: U32}  # exact signed VkResult bit pattern
  Loader{code: U32, message: String}
  InvalidHandle{operation: String}
  InvalidArgument{message: String}
  Unsupported{feature: String}
  EnumerationUnstable{}
  Cleanup{primary: Maybe<Error>, failures: List<Error>}
# InstanceConfig{application_name:String, api_version:U32, layers:List<String>, extensions:List<String>}
# DeviceConfig{queues:List<QueueRequest>, extensions:List<String>}; QueueRequest{family:U32, priorities:List<F32>}
# BufferConfig{size:W.U64, usage:U32}; initially exclusive sharing, zero create flags.
# MemoryAllocateInfo{size:W.U64, memory_type_index:U32}
# MemoryRequirements{size:W.U64, alignment:W.U64, memory_type_bits:U32}
# MemoryProperties includes U64 heap sizes; PhysicalDeviceInfo includes name/type/API and queue families.
def Entry.load() -> IO(Result<&1,&1,U32 & String,Entry>):
  import "./native.c"
  import "./native.js"
def Vk.with_entry(-A: Type, f: Entry -> Vk<A>) -> Vk<A>  # normalize bootstrap errors; always close
# Entry.create_instance(Entry, InstanceConfig) -> Vk<Instance>
# Instance.enumerate_physical_devices(Instance) -> Vk<List<PhysicalDevice>>
# Instance.describe_all(Instance, List<PhysicalDevice>) -> Vk<List<PhysicalDeviceInfo>>
# Instance.memory_properties(Instance, PhysicalDevice) -> Vk<MemoryProperties>
# Instance.create_device(Instance, PhysicalDevice, DeviceConfig) -> Vk<Device>
# Device.{create_buffer,buffer_requirements,allocate_memory,bind_buffer_memory}: see usage
# Device.write_memory(Device, DeviceMemory, W.U64, List<U32>) -> Vk<Unit>
# Device.read_memory(Device, DeviceMemory, W.U64, W.U64) -> Vk<List<U32>>
# Device.destroy_buffer(Device, Buffer), free_memory(Device, DeviceMemory), destroy(Device) -> Vk<Unit>
# Instance.destroy(Instance), Entry.close(Entry) -> Vk<Unit>
# Pure MemoryType.select(MemoryRequirements, MemoryProperties, U32) -> Maybe<U32>
```
`List<U32>` is a byte sequence here: validate each element <=255, never silently truncate. All Vulkan byte sizes, offsets, requirements, alignment and heap sizes use collections U64. C reconstructs `((uint64_t)hi << 32) | lo`; only allocation/copy lengths are checked against SIZE_MAX and practical return-size limits. Pure unsigned comparison and overflow-safe bounds use both limbs, never collections `le_signed`.

Native Entry rows own a dlopen handle and global PFNs; Instance rows own VkInstance plus instance PFNs; Device rows own VkDevice plus device PFNs. Resolve global functions through vkGetInstanceProcAddr(NULL,...), instance functions through the created instance, and device functions through vkGetDeviceProcAddr. Required missing PFNs fail loading; absent vkEnumerateInstanceVersion means Vulkan 1.0. Tables remain alive until their descendants are gone. This follows ash’s three dispatch levels ([ash Entry](https://docs.rs/ash/latest/ash/struct.Entry.html), [Khronos dispatch](https://docs.vulkan.org/refpages/latest/refpages/source/vkGetInstanceProcAddr.html)).

The native registry assigns a globally unique slot/generation U64 to every row, recording kind, parent, actual Vulkan handle and cleanup state. Slots never reuse a generation after wrap: retire them. Validate constructor layout, key, generation, kind, live ancestor chain and common device/instance before touching native objects. Never cast user U64 bits to VkInstance/VkDevice, a pointer, a PFN or a mapped address. An existing ID is a reference, not an unforgeable security capability; copying it aliases one checked object. Per boundary-discipline, all validation lives at effects; per model-the-domain, native rows represent bound/mapped/freed states explicitly.

Only the Bend event loop executes these native Vulkan effects; no IO.fork or parallel Bend calls submit Vulkan work. The registry is consequently a single writer, with ownership lists per Entry rather than one global teardown list. Independent pure preparation, device ranking, byte generation and result comparisons can use balanced Bend parallel calls. Data handle views avoid fictitious affine/RAII guarantees: dropping a constructor cannot release C allocations; with_entry is the default ownership boundary.

Use the normal constructor ABI (`io_node`, `io_tup`, U64 limbs), never `io_hand` for these types. Register effects with `io_eff` using the installed compiler ABI. `io_done` builds successful Result values; domain Fail constructors contain Error, while `io_fail` is appropriate for Entry.load's specified U32/String bootstrap error. `io_cstr` buffers and temporary marshalled arrays have explicit C frees. C owns temporary Vk structs, sets sType/pNext/counts and keeps strings/arrays alive through each call. JS registers matching effects and returns an explicit native-only error. Compile native executables for integration checks.

## Cleanup and observable behavior

Every successful creation enters its owner ledger before publishing the ID; failure after native creation destroys that object before returning. Explicit child destruction invalidates the ID, repeated close succeeds for an already retired matching ID, and forged/unrelated IDs fail. Destroying a parent with live children reports InvalidArgument; Entry.close is the documented cascading exception. Track binding references: free_memory refuses live bound buffers, and failed binding commits no relationship.
Scope close unmaps any outstanding mapping, destroys buffers, frees memory, destroys devices and instances, then dlcloses Entry; use dependency order, not arbitrary reverse creation order. Preserve the callback's error and collect cleanup failures in Cleanup. Entry.close runs even on Vk Fail, but cannot promise cleanup after process termination or IO.die; examples avoid IO.try inside owned scopes. Parent teardown cannot unload a child's PFNs.
Read/write are convenience operations on already bound host-visible allocations, not exported map pointers: map the whole allocation, validate the requested subrange, copy bytes and unmap on every exit. Noncoherent writes flush and reads invalidate a whole-allocation range while mapped; no concurrent GPU work is supported initially. This hides cache/alignment/pointer handling behind two operations ([mapping rules](https://docs.vulkan.org/refpages/latest/refpages/source/vkMapMemory.html), [flush rules](https://docs.vulkan.org/refpages/latest/refpages/source/vkFlushMappedMemoryRanges.html)).
Enumeration loops use count/query/retry with bounded native retries for VK_INCOMPLETE; positive Vulkan statuses are interpreted by command, never treated as generic success. Preserve raw VkResult bits and command names without inventing a Vulkan error for wrapper validation. Reject unsupported requested versions/extensions/configuration before publishing dispatch objects.

## Module layout and generated path

`src/vulkan.bend` is the public import; `src/vk_types.bend` owns configs/errors/pure selection; `src/dispatch.bend` owns effects and scope helpers; `src/native.c`/`.js` own marshalling/registry/dispatch. Existing `deps/bend-collections` supplies U64. `examples/discover.bend` and `examples/buffer_roundtrip.bend` exercise separate reusable calls. A native runtime compatibility smoke program precedes implementation.
`tools/generate.py` consumes pinned Khronos vk.xml plus a small support manifest and deterministically emits enums, flags, version helpers and PFN table/load lists into `src/generated/`; retain source revision and licenses. Emit only supported commands, fail generation on unknown field shapes, and report unsupported surface explicitly. Keep hand-written memory/config marshalling until the generator has supported pointer-length/lifetime rules; a blanket registry translator is not the first milestone.
`LAWS.bend` specifies unsigned U64 comparison/bounds, memory-type selection soundness and selected failure cases; `PROOF.bend` imports it and proves the pure implementation. Native ABI, Vulkan state and driver behavior remain integration obligations. Before commit run `bend PROOF.bend`, generation freshness, native discovery and 16-byte allocate/bind/write/read/assert/cleanup. Include limb preservation above 2^32 without allocating gigabytes, forged/stale/wrong-parent IDs, injected partial-create failure and zero live registry rows. Validation layers, when installed, must report no ownership/memory errors; software Vulkan is an acceptable explicit integration backend, no available ICD is an explicit unmet prerequisite.

## Tradeoffs accepted and alternatives considered

We accept runtime-checked Data references and a scoped native ledger for concise ash-like calls and reliable error cleanup; callers still choose queues, flags, memory types and lifetimes. The interface hides loader ABI, object validation and marshalling without reducing Vulkan to one demonstration function.
Raw U64 handles/pointers expose invalid-pointer dereferences to ordinary Bend construction; rejected. Affine wrappers without a native ledger expose failure-path leaks and still allow forged constructors; rejected. One opaque GPU/session with only upload/download hides useful requirements/allocation/dispatch choices; rejected for insufficiently reusable capability. Generating the complete Vulkan API immediately hides neither pointer lifetimes nor extension constraints; rejected for an unauditable initial boundary.

## Open questions and next implementation step

Should later command submission retain this checked-reference API or introduce separate affine recording/queue capabilities? Defer until submission exists; current scope needs no user decision. First implement Entry.load/close plus one constructor/U64/error ABI smoke executable, then the dependency-ordered native ledger and discovery-to-memory roundtrip. Synthesis decision belongs to the parent design comparison.
